rationale: This qualitative study (using desktop review and semistructured interviews with 15 public/water officials and 49 residents across five Cameroonian municipalities, coded thematically with descriptive frequency tables) centrally examines the privatization/restructuring of urban water management—specifically the dissolution of state monopoly SNEC and the public-private lease arrangement splitting infrastructure and service delivery between parastatal CamWater and private operator CDE, alongside proposed PPP alternatives (`regulatory_model_ownership`). Secondary governance discussions address full-cost-recovery pricing and lack of income-stratified tariffs (`fees_tariffs_subsidies`), overlapping ministerial mandates and municipal council exclusion under decentralization (`institutional_structure_coordination`), and an NGO lawsuit over billing without supply (`review_redress`), but `regulatory_model_ownership` clearly dominates as the primary exposure. Empirically, the study co-equally evaluates multiple access dimensions (`multiple`), led by `effective_access` (service irregularity, rationing, multi-month shortages, reliance on polluted streams/wells, and distance to sources) alongside `primary_connection` (low piped network coverage in peri-urban neighborhoods) and `economic_access` (high bills and retail water prices).
